book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

chapters.relation: Jason Holt's introduction argues there is a genuine paradox in Leonard Cohen: his songs count both as high-art poetry and as popular folk/pop music, challenging the assumed absolute divide between high and popular art. Holt considers whether film auteur theory - the way Hitchcock elevates genre thriller - resolves the paradox by making Cohen a transcendent auteur, or whether the songs remain gloriously popular without any supra-popular transubstantiation. He rejects mentor Louis Dudek's charge that taking up the guitar betrayed Cohen's poetry, insisting the literary lyrics and pleasing melody are perfect complements.

Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.

Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.

Wieland Schwanebeck surveys the many masculinities in Cohen's songs - spies, soldiers, cowboys, rabbis, captains - and argues they mostly appear broken, mocked, or failing (the losing partisan, the captain whose ship leaks or crew deserts), which puts the 'real man' ideal in doubt. He shows how Cohen's Jewishness plays against stereotypes of the bookish, unathletic Jewish man, usually embraced and then inverted with Socratic irony, as in 'Is This What You Wanted' and 'Lover Lover Lover.' Following Judith Butler's Gender Trouble, he reads Cohen's stage persona - the tailored suit, kneeling, clowning, and erotic ambiguity - as a repeated performance demonstrating that masculinity is 'an imitation without an origin.'

Gary Shapiro treats The Future as a 'lyrical phenomenology' of time that stages multiple temporalities rather than one theory of time. 'The Future' evokes an apocalypse where the katechon - the Biblical restraining force holding back the end - no longer works, while 'Waiting for the Miracle' anatomizes passive deferral in a way Shapiro finds sharper than the Stoic critique of waiting by Seneca and Marcus Aurelius and Nietzsche's 'problem of those who wait,' opposing wasted chronos to the seized kairos of 'First We Take Manhattan.' 'Anthem's' crack that lets the light in gets a Gnostic reading, 'Democracy' is glossed through Derrida's 'democracy to come' as messianic, always-arriving futurity, and 'Closing Time' and 'Always' add honky-tonk eschatology and the vow of eternal love.

Jason Holt defends the serious question of whether Cohen is a good singer against both anti-fans and fandom, arguing that judgments of taste purport to objectivity and cannot be settled by polls or Juno Awards. Borrowing David Hume's standard of taste - ideal critics with strong sense, delicate sentiment, practice, comparison, and freedom from prejudice - he judges Cohen in his 'weight class' as a singer-songwriter and vocal stylist, ranks him between Paul Simon and Bob Dylan, and offers the 'great singer-songwriter argument' that excellence in both crafts implies being at least a good singer. Much dismissal, he argues, is really style prejudice or a category mistake, and he ends by confessing that Cohen's voice saved him from teenage suicide, biasing him in the best possible way.

Adam Auch asks why the 'born with the gift of a golden voice' line of 'Tower of Song' is a joke in Cohen's mouth, a lament in Marianne Faithfull's, and a boast in Tom Jones's. Using indexicals, performer persona, and Paul Grice's conversational maxims, he argues interpretation depends on who sings and how: audiences fill the lyric's 'I' with the persona they associate with the performer, and Cohen's bald-faced flouting of the maxim of sincerity forces the ironic reading. The signature 'L. Cohen' in 'Famous Blue Raincoat' ties that song so tightly to Cohen's persona that cover artists must either inhabit the role (Tori Amos) or rewrite the lyrics (Jennifer Warnes), while post-boom 'Hallelujah' covers by Rufus Wainwright and Alexandra Burke perform it as a straight hymn, losing the tension between earthly and heavenly that Cohen and Jeff Buckley preserve.

Edward Winters answers his sister's question - why listen to such depressing music - through Lorca's duende, the 'black sounds' of deep song that, as Nick Cave says, every true love song must contain. He argues duende resists definition yet is recognizable in Cohen, and connects it to Nietzsche's Dionysian art of participation (war dances, anthems, 'Dance Me to the End of Love') as against Kant's disinterested aesthetic distance, so music can re-enchant a disenchanted world. Via Kant's account of artistic genius and Cohen's testimony that Lorca and six flamenco chords gave him his voice, Winters concludes Cohen's dark, honest beauty has duende - which is why it lifts and tears at the heart rather than depressing.

Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.

Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.

Simon Riches argues that Cohen fuses the erotic with the spiritual - worshipping female beauty as religious experience in 'Light as the Breeze' and 'Night Comes On' - and that this produces conflicted, self-deceiving relationships in songs like 'Famous Blue Raincoat' and 'Chelsea Hotel #2.' Against the classical theory of concepts embodied in Socrates' demand for essences, he deploys Wittgenstein's language games and family resemblance, Wittgensteinian views of religious belief, and Davidson's divided mind to deny that love has a rationally coherent essence. Following Richard Rorty, Cohen emerges as an ironist who rejects any 'final vocabulary' of love, and this very contingency and irony ground his authenticity as a singer of romantic love.

Babette Babich traces the shifting 'you' of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne' through Hegelian thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Empedocles's cycle of Love and Strife, reading the songs' ambiguity (David, Samson, the bound champion) as Cohen's sovereign having-it-both-ways. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity frames the human condition of being what one is not, while Nietzsche - on broken promises, on women and distance, on the Antichrist - supplies both the critique of Cohen's courtly projections onto the feminine Other and the model of singularizing solitude. 'Who by Fire' is read against the Rosh Hashanah prayer Unetanneh Tokef as a song of fate, judgment, and atonement whose closing 'who shall I say is calling?' is quasi-Augustinian and Heideggerian: death singularizes each 'who' at the moment of its claim.

Steven Burns rejects both the Obscenity Reading and a merely Poetical Reading of Beautiful Losers in favor of a Political Reading: the four losers - Saint Catherine Tekakwitha, the constipated Anglophone Historian, the French sensualist F., and the Aboriginal wife Edith - represent Canada's founding peoples on the eve of the 1967 centennial. Defending his view that richer works admit a single 'best reading' (after Anthony Savile's aesthetics of best explanation), he reads F.'s Quebec separatism, the statue bombing, and the novel's orgasm-imagery as allegory of a nation inhibited and failing, in dialogue with George Grant's Lament for a Nation. The epilogue's blonde in the Oldsmobile who says 'I am Isis' signals Cohen's dream of a transformed, liberated Canada - Catherine updated - rather than Grant's lament.

Paweł Dobrosielski and Marcin Napiórkowski read Flowers for Hitler as Cohen's answer to Adorno's dictum that to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric - Cohen writes poetry that self-consciously knows it comes after the end of poetry. Using Freud's distinction between the vocabulary and grammar of dreams, they show the collection is assembled from a small repertoire of recurring images (ovens, ashes, telephones, radios, green grass, Nazi names) whose awkward normality expresses repression: life goes on as if nothing had happened. Arendt's banality of evil, born of the Eichmann trial, is directly alluded to in 'All There Is to Know about Adolf Eichmann,' and the book ends by universalizing Holocaust memory - the poet waking with a number on his forearm, feeling like victim and perpetrator alike - until the grass itself is grown on ashes and every flower is a flower for Hitler.

Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.

Christopher Ketcham narrates a night listening to Dear Heather during a café blackout, in which darkness becomes Eugene Minkowski's 'lived space' - more personal than light, with auditory space as its own dark space - and Cohen's voice leads him down into a shared funk of loss and depression. Through Heidegger he diagnoses his own shrunken, past-bound, thrown existence and reinterprets being-toward-death not as a downward spiral but as being toward his own remaining possibilities, and through Freud's death drive he names the 'unobtrusive death wish' he had let dwell unchallenged in him. The essay closes with a Heideggerian resolve toward resoluteness and future possibility, glimpsing a street-worn 'Suzanne' in the dark as hope rather than absence.

Rachel Haliburton asks what metaphysics underwrites Suzanne's world, where a mind can touch a perfect body. The materialist world inherited from Descartes reduces thoughts, meanings, and purposes to purposeless physical processes in which minds never touch bodies; Aristotle's teleological world, refurbished by Thomas Nagel's Mind and Cosmos, builds purposes into nature and treats subjective experience - what the tea and oranges are like for you - as real in its own right. She argues Suzanne's world, and our own ordinary mall-food-court world, is teleological: consciousness is 'biased towards the marvelous,' and we touch one another's bodies with our minds all the time.

Liam Dempsey uses Cohen's songs and the TV piece I Am a Hotel to test somatic against cognitive theories of emotion. William James's James-Lange thesis - emotions are the perception of bodily change - captures the embodied metaphors everywhere in Cohen (icy and broken hearts, trembling, hunger as lust, pain like iodine), while cognitivists such as Martha Nussbaum, working from the Stoic tradition, explain judgment-laden emotions like lifelong love, jealousy, and betrayal in 'Chelsea Hotel #2,' 'Famous Blue Raincoat,' and 'Paper Thin Hotel.' Following Jenefer Robinson's and Ronald de Sousa's process accounts, he concludes a tear is an intellectual thing only as a complex exchange of parallel systems - bodily arousal interpreted and reassessed by appraisal - so that emotions are, finally, written in the flesh.

Timothy P. Jackson argues Cohen is the closest thing today to a Biblical prophet - a 'strong poet' in Harold Bloom's sense, wearing a coat of many colors drawn from Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Taoism, and Sufism, sustained by an 'epistemic humility' that lives between dogmatism and doubt. Cohen leads Christian texts back to their Hebraic origins, critiques every arrogant nationalism including Israel (Book of Mercy, psalm 27), and gave his Tel Aviv concert profits to Israeli-Palestinian reconciliation. Jackson reads Cohen's equanimity at his business manager's embezzlement trial as forgiveness overcoming resentment, weighs his hesed/agape-style unconditional love against his failures in erotic love, and ends with Cohen's reticence about personal immortality - a prophet for the living.

Bernard Wills takes the reference to The Cloud of Unknowing in 'The Window' as the key to Cohen's lifelong fascination with apophatic, negative mysticism - God sought beyond every image in a 'naked intent of love,' as in the medieval Cloud, Dionysius, Maimonides, and Kabbalah - against the kataphatic way of affirmation. He reads Recent Songs as an album of exile and the play of union and separation ('Un Canadien Errant,' 'Ballad of the Absent Mare'), where the incarnate Word is 'stuttered' and 'frozen,' a passion without resurrection. Cohen's later Zen turn is thus prefigured: the emptiness of sunyata and the Neo-Platonic descent from and return to the One are positive nothingness - self-overcoming in the service of compassion rather than the black-romantic nihilism of self-annihilation.

Peter Stone applies Dawkins's memetics and Dennett's Breaking the Spell to the rise of 'Hallelujah' from the troubled release of Various Positions to ubiquity via John Cale, Jeff Buckley, Shrek, and Rufus Wainwright. On Dennett's account religious memes thrive through hyperactive agency detection, doctrines rendered unfalsifiable and thus immune to evidence, and 'belief in belief' - and 'Hallelujah' is religiously ambiguous enough, from David and Bathsheba to Buckley's 'hallelujah of the orgasm,' to be as religious as any singer or congregation wants it to be, whether as Rabbi Kagan's hymn of the heretic or the Holy Trinity Church's 'Amazing Grace' lyric swap. Machiavelli's maxim that fortune governs half the outcome frames the song's lucky trajectory, and its carefully engineered ambiguity makes it a set of very 'happy memes' likely to keep replicating.

holes.name: The Katechon (the restraining force)
holes.what: From 2 Thessalonians, the force that restrains the coming of the Antichrist and holds back the end of the world, later a key idea in political theology.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads the song 'The Future' as announcing that the katechon no longer works so the apocalyptic end has already arrived; no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Gnosticism
holes.what: A religious worldview in which the world is the flawed work of a lesser or malevolent demiurge and salvation comes through sparks of divine light escaping it.
holes.why: Chapter 14 asks 'Is Cohen a Gnostic?' and reads 'Anthem's' light getting in through the cracks as a Gnostic metaphor, a tradition the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Paul Grice
holes.what: Philosopher of language known for the conversational maxims and implicature, showing how context and speaker expectations generate meaning beyond the words uttered.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Grice's maxim of sincerity to explain why the 'golden voice' line of 'Tower of Song' is ironic in Cohen's mouth but a boast in Tom Jones's.

holes.name: Conversational Implicature
holes.what: Meaning a speaker conveys by flouting conversational expectations rather than stating it outright, leaving hearers to work out what is meant.
holes.why: Chapter 17's core tool for explaining how covers change what a Cohen lyric communicates through persona, signature, and performance context.

holes.name: Duende
holes.what: Lorca's 'black sounds': the dark, primordial emotional power that authentic art - flamenco deep song, the true love song - must channel, likened in the chapter to Nietzsche's Dionysian.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues Cohen's songs have duende, which is why they hearten rather than depress; no taxonomy slug covers this aesthetic concept.

holes.name: Socratic Irony
holes.what: Ostentatious self-concealment in speech that makes hearers grasp the gap between words and intentions, analyzed by Kierkegaard in The Concept of Irony as a way of building personality and intimacy.
holes.why: Chapter 20's central claim is that Cohen seduces through Socratic irony; the taxonomy's elenchus and Socratic-ignorance slugs do not capture irony itself.

holes.name: Empedocles
holes.what: Pre-Socratic thinker who explained the cosmos through an eternal cycle in which Love unites and Strife separates the elements.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the 'Empedocles effect' - the alternation of love and strife - as a central frame for the ambivalence of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne.'

holes.name: Eugene Minkowski
holes.what: Phenomenological psychiatrist known for analyses of lived time and lived space, including auditory space as a dark, intimate space that envelops the self.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds its entire reading of Dear Heather around Minkowski's concepts of lived space and dark space, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Richard Dawkins
holes.what: Evolutionary theorist who introduced the 'meme' in The Selfish Gene: cultural units that replicate and compete for human attention the way genes compete in nature.
holes.why: Chapter 35 explains the spread of 'Hallelujah' through Dawkins's memetics; the taxonomy has Dennett but not Dawkins.

holes.name: Memetics (cultural evolution)
holes.what: The theory that cultural units - songs, theories, catchphrases - evolve by differential survival in human attention, as genes do in nature.
holes.why: Chapter 35's explanation of why 'Hallelujah' conquered popular culture is explicitly memetic; the taxonomy has no concept for cultural evolution.
